detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates that a rational inattention-based cognitive resource allocation model provides a consistent explanation for numerous empirical facts regarding context effects and choice overload that have been repeatedly observed in the literature. Notably, the model yields predictions consistent with observed data not only for the phenomena themselves but also for the cognitive dimensions of the decisionmaker, such as shifts in attention and declines in choice satisfaction. While context effects and choice overload have traditionally developed as independent fields due to their apparent inconsistency with rational choice models in economics, the model proposed in this study offers a unified framework for analyzing these phenomena and their associated marketing strategies through an approach grounded in utility maximization.

title: Consumer Rights and Algorithms
affiliations: University of Nebraska at Lincoln - College of Law

detail.title: Consumer Rights and Algorithms
detail.abstract: This article summarizes the field of consumer protection law, from its historical roots to the contemporary challenges of the digital age. It outlines the legal doctrines governing consumer deception and unfair trade practices, highlighting the interplay between common-law, statutory, and private modes of regulation. The article then addresses the impact of artificial intelligence and big data on consumer markets, focusing on digital advertising and new forms of consumer fraud. Finally, it explores regulatory responses to these challenges, including data privacy laws and prohibitions on dark patterns, which illustrate the trade-offs inherent in consumer protection frameworks.

title: Fear Gauges and Oil Futures: Weekday Patterns in Volatility Spillovers
affiliations: University College Dublin, Dublin City University  and

detail.title: Fear Gauges and Oil Futures: Weekday Patterns in Volatility Spillovers
detail.abstract: We examine how implied volatility and volatility-of-volatility in US and Euro area equity markets (VIX, VVIX, VSTOXX, VVSTOXX) transmit to crude and refined oil futures (light gasoil, gasoline, heating oil, Brent, WTI) using a TVP-VAR connectedness framework and an EGARCH-in-mean model of connectedness. Linkages are found to be strong, but heterogeneous: VIX-WTI, VVIX-gasoil and VSTOXX/VVSTOXX-gasoline and heating oil dominate, with volatility-of-volatility indices generating the most tail-intensive spillovers. Connectedness changes are mean-reverting with persistent conditional volatility, display weaker Monday and stronger Friday spillovers, and rise with realised skewness, yielding contract-specific, regionally segmented, calendar-dependent transmission with implications for hedging, margin setting and financial stability.

title: Does the Informal Economy Undermine Political Stability? Empirical Evidence from Global Perspectives
affiliations: Sakarya University - Department of Economics, Fort Hays State University, University of Florida, International Islamic University Chittagong (IIUC) and University of Georgia - Department of Agricultural & Applied Economics

detail.title: Does the Informal Economy Undermine Political Stability? Empirical Evidence from Global Perspectives
detail.abstract: Political stability (PS) is a cornerstone of economic development, yet the role of the informal economy (IE) in determining PS remains unexplored in literature. This study addresses this significant gap by examining how informal and formal economies (FE) influence PS across 124 countries from 1996 to 2018. Using the method of moments quantile regression (MMQR) and advanced econometric techniques, the research finds that while the IE significantly undermines PS, the FE plays a vital role in enhancing PS. These results offer valuable insights for policymakers, emphasizing the importance of minimizing IE activities as a means to ensure PS and promote sustainable economic development. This research also underscores the need for targeted policy interventions to promote FE activities and strengthen institutional frameworks, ensuring long-term PS and sustainable development.

title: The Age of Content: How Content Fuels Protests on Visual Social Media
affiliations: Ifo Institute, Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB) and University of Zurich

detail.title: The Age of Content: How Content Fuels Protests on Visual Social Media
detail.abstract: How does the nature of social media content shape the diffusion of protest? This paper provides causal evidence from the 2023 Nahel riots in France, a nationwide wave of unrest triggered by a police killing and propelled by online mobilization. Using data on 537 protest events and more than 50,000 geolocated Instagram interactions, we construct a municipality-by-day panel of social media exposure. Our identification strategy leverages exogenous variation in pre-riot Instagram connectivity-measured via residualized comment flows on a network seeded on football celebrities' posts-to isolate the diffusion of protest through online ties. We find that digital exposure to protest in connected municipalities significantly increases the probability of local protest, with effects concentrated the following day. Beyond volume, we show that protest diffusion is content-dependent. Pro-movement, emotionally salient, and visually prominent posts are particularly effective at promoting both online engagement and offline action, while exposure to fear-inducing or repressive imagery discourages protest despite increasing attention. Posts with coordination cues (explicit calls to action or protest logistics) have the strongest mobilizing effects. Our findings show that image-based social media accelerate protest diffusion not only by lowering coordination barriers but also by amplifying emotional cues. They reveal how emotional tone, political alignment, and visual structure jointly condition the spread of digital protest.

title: Concentration in Food Retailing, Prices, and Greedflation
affiliations: University of Minnesota - St. Paul - Department of Applied Economics, , North Dakota State University, Government of the United States of America - Office of the Chief Economist and United States Department of Agriculture, Fort Collins

detail.title: Concentration in Food Retailing, Prices, and Greedflation
detail.abstract: We examine whether food price inflation differs by market concentration across a sample of urban Core-Based Statistical Areas in the United States. Market concentration is measured using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, constructed from sales data from the National Establishment Time Series, which provides a near-census of food retail establishments. Price data come from UPC-level point-of-sale scanner records for major food categories-produce, dairy, meat, and non-alcoholic beverages-covering the period from 2009 to 2022. Using panel data methods with instrumental variables, we find a positive and significant association between market concentration and price levels during the study period. However, when comparing the preinflation period with the inflationary phase (June 2021-2022), the association turns negative and significant, indicating that prices in more concentrated markets increased more slowly. Contrary to the prevailing "greedflation" narrative, our results indicate that higher food retail market concentration may have mitigated rather than amplified the recent food price inflation episode.

title: Beyond Demand Estimation: Consumer Surplus Evaluation via Cumulative Propensity Weights
affiliations: Florida State University, University of Virginia - Darden School of Business, University of Texas at Dallas and George Washington University - School of Business

detail.title: Beyond Demand Estimation: Consumer Surplus Evaluation via Cumulative Propensity Weights
detail.abstract: This paper develops a practical framework for using observational data to audit the consumer surplus effects of AI-driven decisions, specifically in targeted pricing and algorithmic lending. Traditional approaches first estimate demand functions and then integrate to compute consumer surplus, but these methods can be challenging to implement in practice due to model misspecification in parametric demand forms and the large data requirements and slow convergence of flexible nonparametric or machine learning approaches. Instead, we exploit the randomness inherent in modern algorithmic pricing, arising from the need to balance exploration and exploitation, and introduce an estimator that avoids explicit estimation and numerical integration of the demand function. Each observed purchase outcome at a randomized price is an unbiased estimate of demand and by carefully reweighting purchase outcomes using novel cumulative propensity weights (CPW), we are able to reconstruct the integral, or area under demand curve, when these outcomes are aggregated. Building on this idea, we introduce a doubly robust variant named the augmented cumulative propensity weighting (ACPW) estimator that only requires one of either the demand model or the historical pricing policy distribution to be correctly specified. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the use of flexible machine learning methods for estimating consumer surplus, since it achieves fast convergence rates by incorporating an estimate of demand, even when the machine learning estimate has slower convergence rates. Neither of these estimators is a standard application of off-policy evaluation techniques, since the target estimand, consumer surplus, is typically unobserved. To address algorithmic fairness, we extend this framework to an inequality-aware surplus measure, allowing regulators and firms to quantify the tradeoff between firm profit and equity. Finally, we conduct a comprehensive numerical study to validate the theoretical properties of our proposed methods.

detail.abstract:
Financial governance in multinational organizations requires a robust integration of risk management, operational controls, and data quality standards. As companies expand across regions such as North America (NAM), Latin America (LATAM), Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA), and the Asia-Pacific (APAC), decentralized structures often generate inconsistencies in financial reporting, fragmented accountability, and recurrent control failures.

This paper proposes an integrated governance framework that unifies Data Quality Assurance (DQA), control execution, remediation processes, and oversight mechanisms into a coordinated model suitable for global financial operations. Drawing on applied methodologies commonly utilized in large financial institutions, the model strengthens accuracy, transparency, and regulatory compliance. It also provides a scalable structure that mitigates operational risk and enhances alignment across regional units. The proposed framework offers practical and replicable guidance for multinational organizations seeking to elevate the integrity of their financial governance systems.

title: Joint Investigation Response Protocol (JIRP) A Non-Collapsing Protocol for LLM Alignment Tasks

detail.title: Joint Investigation Response Protocol (JIRP) A Non-Collapsing Protocol for LLM Alignment Tasks
detail.abstract: This technical note introduces the Joint Investigation Response Protocol (JIRP), a non-collapsing alignment behavior that replaces the collapse tendency exhibited by large language models during self-referential evaluation. The protocol includes a prompt template, a collapse index (CI), and a fidelity scoring rubric (JFS) designed to enable immediate replication and adversarial testing.

detail.abstract: This study conducts a comparative cross-sector analysis of 122 publicly listed companies across 11 major industries in India and the US. Using long-term forecasts (2025-2030), ROCE-based efficiency measures, valuation frameworks (DCF, RIM, and relative multiples), and multi-factor scorecards, the research examines structural differences in profitability, reinvestment efficiency, capital productivity, and long-term sectoral fundamentals. Heatmaps, ROCE-P/E scatter models, and sector scorecards identify undervalued sectors and highlight sustained performance patterns across both economies. Results suggest that India's Defence, Industrials, Auto, FMCG, and Energy sectors exhibit strong ROCE resilience and long-term growth potential, while US Technology, Utilities, and Communication Services demonstrate superior reinvestment efficiency and valuation stability. The findings indicate that combining India's structural upside with the US's stable, high-quality profit pools provides a balanced long-term allocation framework. The study contributes to cross-market investment understanding by integrating sector fundamentals, macro drivers, and valuation-based outlooks for the decade ahead.

title: A Theory of Stochastic Arbitrage: Identification and Inference in Incomplete Markets

detail.title: A Theory of Stochastic Arbitrage: Identification and Inference in Incomplete Markets
detail.abstract: This paper develops a general theory for testing the feasibility of dynamic arbitrage in markets with frictions and significant model uncertainty. I posit a paradigm shift: arbitrage feasibility is a property encoded not in ex-post portfolio profitability, but in the time-series properties of a latent price differential. I establish the Stochastic Arbitrage Criterion (SAC), a formal condition requiring this latent differential to be a stationary process with a predictable conditional mean, ensuring mispricing is transitory. The core econometric challenge is that this latent process is observed with non-classical measurement error from a misspecified theoretical model. I propose a novel state-space filtering framework to disentangle the true arbitrage signal from persistent model error. I prove global identification of the key parameters from the auto-covariance structure and provide robust inference procedures, including a valid parametric bootstrap for the composite null hypothesis, validated by extensive Monte Carlo evidence. The framework provides a unifying lens to classify market regimesfrom strong efficiency to stochastic arbitrage and model failure-and generalizes beyond my central application to capital structure arbitrage, offering a new toolkit for dynamically assessing the limits of arbitrage.

title: Section 230 and Social Media Immunity
affiliations: University of Nebraska at Lincoln - College of Law

detail.title: Section 230 and Social Media Immunity
detail.abstract:
Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act is often credited—only slightly hyperbolically—with having “created the internet.” It did so by insulating online intermediaries from liability for third-party speech, thereby enabling platforms to host user content at scale. But the doctrinal story is more complicated, and the modern controversy is less about first principles than about fit. This chapter situates Section 230 in the pre-internet common law of defamation and republication, where courts developed conduit and distributor rules to avoid imposing impossible monitoring burdens on mass communications systems. Against that backdrop, Congress enacted Section 230 as part of the Communications Decency Act, aiming to encourage voluntary content moderation without triggering publisher-like liability. Early courts then converted a textually ambiguous provision into an expansive immunity doctrine, extending protection beyond classic publication claims and into a wide range of modern “hybrid” wrongs—cases where platforms’ design choices, algorithms, or business practices interact with user misconduct.

The result is an immunity regime that is both essential and increasingly strained. With Congress politically deadlocked, reform pressure has shifted to the Supreme Court, which—having never squarely interpreted Section 230—retains unusual freedom to recalibrate the doctrine. This chapter maps the interpretive moves that produced today’s breadth and sketches the legal terrain that would remain if the Court narrows immunity: traditional pleading constraints, proximate cause limits, and common-law conduit defenses that can protect the internet without making it unaccountable.

title: Soft Budget Constraints and Public–Private Partnerships: An Empirical Analysis of Brazilian Municipalities (1999–2024)
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Soft Budget Constraints and Public–Private Partnerships: An Empirical Analysis of Brazilian Municipalities (1999–2024)
detail.abstract: Public–Private Partnerships (PPPs) have been widely used as a policy instrument to support infrastructure investment under fiscal constraints. This study examines the effects of PPP adoption on the fiscal dynamics of Brazilian municipalities between 1999 and 2024. Using an annual municipal panel, it estimates causal impacts through the staggered Difference-in-Differences estimator proposed by Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), with never-treated municipalities serving as the control group. The analysis focuses on key fiscal outcomes, including current revenues, intergovernmental transfers, own-source tax revenues, current expenditures, and debt service. The results show that PPP adoption is associated with a substantial and persistent reduction in municipal debt service, without evidence of a significant expansion in current expenditures, alongside moderate declines in revenues, taxes, and transfers. This pattern is consistent with a substitution of explicit public debt by long-term contractual obligations and a rebalancing of the municipal financing mix. Dynamic specifications, placebo tests, and the absence of systematic pre-trends support the credibility of the identification strategy. Overall, the study provides recent empirical evidence on the medium-term fiscal trade-offs associated with the use of PPPs as a tool for municipal fiscal management.

title: Economic Rationale of Subsidizing Federal Loans through Fiscal Externalities
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: Economic Rationale of Subsidizing Federal Loans through Fiscal Externalities
detail.abstract: A fiscal externality occurs when the normal activities of a business affect government revenue. When positive fiscal externalities are not fully recognized or credited, firms tend to underprovide those activities, resulting in lower government revenue than would otherwise occur. Below, we justify why the federal government has a strong incentive to subsidize and fund federal loans by explicitly accounting for fiscal externalities and outline a two part program to achieve this aim.

title: Simulated Justice: How AI Alignment Replaces Conflict with Coherence
affiliations: , Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST)

detail.title: Simulated Justice: How AI Alignment Replaces Conflict with Coherence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: What if the danger of legal AI is not that it misjudges, but that it sounds perfectly judicious? As legal value alignment becomes a central goal in the design of large language models (LLMs), these systems increasingly produce outputs that appear lawful, balanced, and procedurally sound. But behind their rhetorical fluency lies a powerful illusion: the simulation of legal judgment without its institutional or political substance. This paper critiques alignment not as a failure, but as a success too well executed, one that replaces legal disagreement with semantic symmetry, and recasts justice as an output format. Drawing on jurisprudential theory and discourse analysis, we show how AI answers flatten normative conflict into technocratic equilibrium, offering “reasonable” positions that obscure power, silence dissent, and domesticate law’s agonistic core. Through examples such as hate speech, surrogacy, and criminal responsibility, we expose how alignment displaces the burden of choice with the comfort of coherence. In response, the paper proposes an anti-alignment jurisprudence, one that values contestation over calibration, and treats law not as a language model’s task, but as a political act that must remain interruptible. In doing so, the paper cautions against the growing role of generative AI as a source of normative authority, not because it gets law wrong, but because it sounds too much like it gets it right.

title: Reframing Business Value from a Philosophical Perspective Long-Term Sustainable Human Cooperation as the Foundation of Value Networks and Stakeholder Analysis
affiliations: Fan Ge Institute

detail.title: Reframing Business Value from a Philosophical Perspective Long-Term Sustainable Human Cooperation as the Foundation of Value Networks and Stakeholder Analysis
detail.abstract:
Mainstream business analysis frameworks tend to reduce value to revenue growth, market share, or shareholder returns. However, a growing number of business decisions that appear internally coherent and economically rational in the short term increasingly result in long-term consequences such as erosion of trust, organizational dysfunction, regulatory backlash, and systemic instability. 
This paper argues that such failures are not primarily problems of execution, but of judgment-specifically, of neglected value foundations. Drawing on philosophical value theory and theories of social cooperation, the paper proposes that the fundamental function of business value is not short-term profit maximization, but the maintenance of conditions that enable long-term sustainable human cooperation. 
The paper develops a three-layer model of business value-value experience, value principles, and value beliefs-and reconceptualizes value networks as cooperation structures rather than mere flows of capital or resources. Four critical but often overlooked dimensions of value circulation are introduced: value creation flows, trust flows, risk allocation flows, and dignity flows. Building on this framework, the paper reconstructs stakeholder analysis as a normative stress test of cooperation sustainability rather than a prioritization of power or influence.
By repositioning business as a form of social practice that continuously shapes modes of cooperation, this study reconnects philosophy, humanism, and strategic decision-making, offering a stable evaluative framework for long-term business sustainability in complex environments.

title: The Rise of Anti-Oligarchy and Its Limits in Backsliding Indonesia

detail.title: The Rise of Anti-Oligarchy and Its Limits in Backsliding Indonesia
detail.abstract: Indonesia's recent democratic decline has unfolded alongside a growing public critique of oligarchy and elite capture. While existing studies have documented the consolidation of politicobusiness power within state institutions, far less is known about how ordinary citizens perceive this process and whether rising anti-oligarchic sentiment functions as a force for democratic resistance. This study addresses this gap by introducing an original Anti-Oligarchy Index (AOI) based on nationally representative survey data, capturing public perceptions of elite domination, unequal access to power, and biased law enforcement. The findings show that anti-oligarchic sentiment in Indonesia is widespread, socially patterned, and politically attentive. It is strongest among younger, urban, and educated citizens and translates into clear opposition to elite-driven economic policies, most notably the Omnibus Law on Job Creation. Anti-oligarchy thus reflects a form of substantive resistance grounded in demands for fairness and economic justice, rather than diffuse dissatisfaction or political apathy. However, the study also reveals clear limits to this opposition. While elite-critical citizens are highly sensitive to distributive injustice, they display weaker commitment to democratic norms, conditional support for civil liberties, and growing skepticism toward representative institutions. As a result, opposition to oligarchic power remains politically fragmented and normatively ambivalent. The study concludes that anti-oligarchy in Indonesia constitutes resistance without democratic anchoring-capable of contesting elite outcomes but insufficient to sustain democratic defense.

title: From Procedural Completeness to Audit-Proof Security: The Public Disclosure Gap in Rules Governing the Disclosure of Foreign-Related Impacts and Agency Relationships by Legislative Proposal Submitters to the National People's Congress
affiliations: Dhurakij Pundit University

detail.title: From Procedural Completeness to Audit-Proof Security: The Public Disclosure Gap in Rules Governing the Disclosure of Foreign-Related Impacts and Agency Relationships by Legislative Proposal Submitters to the National People's Congress
detail.abstract: This paper employs the OSINT evidence auditing methodology for normative texts, using publicly available and verifiable normative documents as the evidentiary boundary. It examines the configuration of disclosure rules governing foreign influence and agency relationships of proposal entities during the legislative proposal stage of the National People's Congress and its Standing Committee. Through clause-by-clause verification of authoritative texts including the Legislation Law and the Rules of Procedure of the NPC/NPCSC, this study finds that current disclosure rules adequately address meeting procedures and the structure of attached materials versus exceptions. However, they fail to codify provisions concerning disclosure of foreign influence/agency relationships, the entities and standards for tiered verification, and the closed-loop audit trail field. Guided by the principle of proportionality, this paper proposes a minimal closed-loop solution comprising 'minimum disclosure set-tiered verification-audit trail-security exceptions/remedies'. It provides a set of trigger conditions, threshold calibration mechanisms, and an audit field dictionary directly embeddable into regulations to support the upgrade of legislative security through auditability. Furthermore, the Explanatory Notes on the Draft Amendment to the Legislation Law of the People's Republic of China indicate that the amendment seeks to strengthen disclosure of 'explanatory statements and reports' alongside constitutional review information: For instance, it mandates that explanatory notes to draft laws include relevant opinions concerning constitutionality issues. It further requires timely publication of legal texts, announcements, draft explanatory notes, deliberation outcome reports, and other materials in the Gazette of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress and on the NPC website, thereby providing institutional interfaces for establishing 'audit-safe' rule-based traceability. However, this explanatory note itself does not constitute a mandatory provision for disclosing and verifying 'proposing entities' foreign-related impacts/agency relationships'. The Rules of Procedure of the National People's Congress of the People's Republic of China further stipulate: When a delegation or 30 or more deputies jointly propose a bill, the Presidium shall decide whether to include it in the agenda. For bills included in the agenda, the proposers and relevant institutions 'shall provide relevant materials,' and the proposers 'shall submit an explanatory statement on the bill.' Concurrently, meetings shall be held publicly as a principle, with closed sessions permitted when necessary, establishing an 'open-as-a-rule, closed-as-an-exception' institutional framework.

title: A Neuro-Adaptive AI Framework for Interrupting High-Risk Speculative Trading and Restoring Self-Regulation

detail.title: A Neuro-Adaptive AI Framework for Interrupting High-Risk Speculative Trading and Restoring Self-Regulation
detail.abstract: The increased accessibility of retail trading has led to broader market participation across diverse demographic groups. This expansion, however, underscores a significant yet frequently overlooked concern: the psychological impact of trading. Structural features such as high leverage, margin access, and platform design often create trading environments that mirror gambling dynamics. These conditions may foster maladaptive behaviours, including overtrading, revenge trading, and loss-chasing. Such behaviours threaten financial stability and are closely linked to adverse mental health outcomes, including anxiety and depression. This paper presents a conceptual framework for an artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot designed to address the mental health needs of retail traders. The framework integrates principles from affective computing, behavioural finance, and digital mental health interventions to identify and mitigate stress-induced and compulsive trading behaviours. The proposed system employs real-time detection of risky patterns by analyzing behavioural and linguistic signals, as well as deviations from pre-established user trading plans. It then delivers personalized, evidence-based interventions grounded in cognitive-behavioural and mindfulness techniques. By incorporating transparent ethical safeguards and aligning interventions with self-imposed constraints, this approach utilizes advanced machine learning to provide adaptive and timely support, thereby reducing psychological risks and promoting responsible trading practices within the financial sector.

title: Team Operations and Peer Reporting: Pulling the "Andon Cord" on Loyalty
affiliations: University of Utah and University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business

detail.title: Team Operations and Peer Reporting: Pulling the "Andon Cord" on Loyalty
detail.abstract: Team operations are ubiquitous and have the following features: (i) The output is jointly determined by efforts of individual team members; and (ii) team members, but not the principal, can observe the effort of their peers (hence the principal cannot identify shirkers). Together these give rise to free riding that exacerbates moral hazard in teams-observing that peers are exerting effort, an individual team member is more likely to shirk. It is well acknowledged that moral hazard is a particularly vexing problem in team operations. One remedy to alleviate moral hazard in teams is peer reporting, where team members that exert effort can report shirkers to the principal. As we show, peer reporting eliminates moral hazard in teams, and emerges endogenously in equilibrium even when it benefits the principal but not the agents, and even when the principal does not commit to a reward for peer reporting. However, a key barrier to peer reporting is loyalty: team members who feel a sense of loyalty towards peers are disinclined to report shirking. Using the framework of dynamic team games, we demonstrate that even a small probability of encountering a loyal teammate can trigger widespread shirking that goes unreported even by those team members who are not loyal. Paradoxically, loyalty, an exalted value, backfires due to the strategic externalities that it imposes on other members of the team. Interventions that destigmatize peer reporting and shed a more nuanced light on the value of loyalty (such as the Andon cord in the Toyota Production System) can alleviate this problem. Our paper, incorporating incentives, information and morality, shows that it is time for organizations to pull the 'Andon Cord' on the misplaced morality of loyalty to peers.

title: 'Scaling Laws' and Interoperability as the Backbone of the Digital Economy
affiliations: New York University - Leonard N. Stern School of Business - Department of Economics , University College London - Faculty of Laws and Stanford University

detail.title: 'Scaling Laws' and Interoperability as the Backbone of the Digital Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest. Personal views, do not engage the CAT.

detail.abstract:
We examine when interoperability should serve as a structural response to market concentration produced by scaling laws, network effects, and data driven complementarities and capabilities in the digital economy. Digital infrastructures such as operating systems, cloud platforms, payments, and AI systems exhibit superlinear returns to scale that interact with multi-sided feedback loops to generate dominant positions and persistent bottlenecks. However, interoperability can also dilute beneficial complementarities, create security and privacy risks, and in some cases weaken incentives to invest.  The paper makes two contributions. First, we develop a conceptual framework that treats digital ecosystems as lattices of complementarities linking users, developers, data, and infrastructure. Scaling laws are empirical signatures of supermodular relationships. Interoperability becomes a lattice restructuring tool that selectively weakens complementarities that entrench market (economic) power while preserving those that support quality, safety, and innovation. Second, we pair this economic account with a comparative analysis of legal and institutional approaches to interoperability. Examples include telecom interconnection, the Microsoft antitrust cases, the EU Digital Markets Act and Data Act, digital health regulation in the EU and the US, and emerging sector specific regimes in blockchain and AI. This comparison clarifies how horizontal and vertical interoperability obligations distribute network (complex systems) complementarities across layers and how ex ante and ex post tools differ in their ability to reshape digital ecosystems. We also argue that interoperability has emerged in the EU as a broader legal principle enshrined across multiple areas of law, including competition law and digital regulation. 
In sum, we provide a unified view of interoperability as a family of interventions that determine which complementarities are internalized by a single platform and which are shared across rivals and customers. Effective policy requires aligning the locus of interoperability with the structure of complementarities and the risks of fragmentation.

title: Fiscal Geometry as Structural Grammar in Regulatory Workflows :  A Neutral, Reusable Representation Layer between Execution and Judgment

detail.abstract: Regulatory authorities operate at the intersection of two persistent mandates: public-finance enforcement and the supervision of private capital behavior across borders, institutions, and rule regimes. In the digital and AI era, the operational problem is rarely a shortage of rules. It is the representational condition of regulatory material itself: information is abundant but fragmented; reporting systems are heterogeneous; cases span multiple agencies and timeframes; and review must remain defensible under pressure. As a result, regulatory work frequently depends on narrative reconstruction across scattered artifacts rather than on a stable, reusable representational baseline. This working paper introduces a supplementary structural grammar for regulatory analysis that operates prior to aggregation, scoring, or normative evaluation. The grammar provides an interface layer for rendering heterogeneous regulatory materials into consistent, reviewable structures—such as event nodes, procedural gates, pathway sequences, and recurring bottleneck configurations—so that cross-case comparability and internal review become tractable without changing the substantive standards applied by the regulator. The proposed approach is explicitly assistive rather than substitutive. It does not prescribe legal conclusions, evidentiary thresholds, or enforcement actions, and it does not require a new dataset or a new compliance regime. Instead, it offers a transferable representation protocol that strengthens institutional traceability and analytical consistency while preserving the sovereignty of professional judgment and accountability within existing regulatory mandates.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether private equity can function as a catalyst for economic stability and growth in developing countries. It argues that private equity contributes to development by providing long-term capital, improving corporate governance, fostering entrepreneurship, and supporting job creation in economies where traditional financial systems are weak. The study outlines structural causes of economic instability, including limited access to finance, institutional inefficiencies, and regulatory uncertainty. It then analyzes how private equity differs from traditional bank financing and evaluates its effectiveness through comparative case studies, including the United States, Kenya, and Colombia. While private equity carries governance and regulatory risks, the findings suggest that when paired with institutional reform, it can support long-term economic stability and modernization in developing economies.

title: Sustainable Development Goals Omission and Environmental Sentiment Metric for Greenwashing and ESG Controversies Alert in Green Bonds

detail.abstract: Green bonds are a cornerstone of sustainable finance, directing investment toward projects that support environmental objectives and the transition to a low-carbon economy. Yet, the growing risk of greenwashing threatens to undermine the credibility of such instruments. Greenwashing refers to situations where sustainability-related statements do not clearly and fairly reflect, (i.e., through the omission of material information), the underlying sustainability profile of an entity or financial product. The development of robust analytical tools to assess the credibility of issuers’ sustainability claims plays a key role in ensuring that green bond financing genuinely contributes to measurable environmental outcomes, rather than serving merely as a vehicle for reputational enhancement. These tools also support more effective supervision thereby helping to prevent the risk of misleading investors and weakening market trust. Leveraging a combination of dictionary-based techniques and domain specific BERT transformer models, we explore how the omission of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) content in corporate disclosure relates to the volume and tone of environmental and SDGs specific language in the sustainability reports of green bonds issuers. To this purpose, we developed two new metrics that allow to systematically assess the link between the disclosure and the risk of misleading sustainability claims and information omission. The first indicator, the Sustainable Development Goals Omission Index (SDGOI), shows that an opportunity-oriented tone in general environmental sentences is positively associated with SDGs omission, potentially representing a distinctive trait of greenwashing risk. Therefore, we introduced the Environmental Sentiment Metric (ESM), a novel indicator that quantifies opportunity-oriented environmental sentiment and connects it to greenwashing accusations and ESG controversies. We found that elevated ESM scores are significantly associated with higher ESG controversy levels and with greenwashing accusations, demonstrating its potential as an alert signal of disclosure credibility risks in the green bond market. Integrating these indicators into the infrastructure of sustainable finance can provide investors and regulators with analytical tools for assessing sustainability disclosures, while encouraging issuers to report transparently and accountably – thereby enhancing the effectiveness and integrity of capital markets.

title: Music Metadata Governance: A Legal Perspective

detail.title: Music Metadata Governance: A Legal Perspective

detail.abstract: The governance of music (meta)data, meaning the rules and institutions governing (meta)data access and transferability within the music sector, constitutes a significant yet under-explored facet of the music data lifecycle. This chapter delves into the legal framework applicable to music (meta)data, with a particular emphasis on European data law. The analysis reveals that three areas of attention. The first refers to rules on data access and portability which, while not directly applicable to music (meta)data, could represent important sources of inspiration for future statutory or voluntary interventions. The second area refers to the novel rules on unfair contractual terms in data contracts. These rules are not specific to the music sector, but will certainly apply to any contract, including in the music sector, when the object of the contract is a qualifying data access or use provision. The third area refers to data intermediation services (DIS), a category that, while being at the core of the EU data strategy, has not yet performed as expected (and may be soon revised). DIS rules may apply to orchestrators of music (meta)data services depending on their specific features. Given the non trivial requirements under which DIS are subjected to, it will be important to ascertain their applicability and arguably design the relevant services accordingly.

title: Deepfake & Deepfaith
affiliations: and Carnegie Mellon University - School of Computer Science

detail.title: Deepfake & Deepfaith
detail.abstract:
In the age of deepfake, we need deepfaith in ourselves. Unlike most deepfake studies that catastrophize deepfakes’ impacts, this Article critically examines deepfakes’ impacts on the information marketplace dynamics and the truth-seeking objectives from a transtemporal lens. To that end, This Article evaluates the inter-informational competitive relationship between visual representations and word-based statements. In the Pre-Deepfake Age, visual representation was the most competitive information type in the truth-seeking marketplace, surpassing word-based factual statements and opinions. However, the prevalence of deepfakes is revolutionizing the already established inter-informational competitive order. From this perspective, this Article categorizes the deepfakes’ incursions into two phases: Deepfake 1.0 and Deepfake 2.0.

In Deepfake 1.0, the widespread diffusion of generative AI has significantly lowered the technical barriers to creating fabricated audiovisual content, making authentication and falsification nearly impossible. In the absence of sufficient, reliable information sources, individuals lacking necessary technical tools or literacy skills have to bear overwhelming cognitive burdens when confronted with persuasive yet deceptive content. As a result, the prevalence of deepfakes weakens the competitiveness of visual representation in the truth-seeking marketplace and distorts the longstanding inter-informational competitive hierarchy among visual representation, factual statement, and normative opinion. This unwelcome tendency forces numerous First Amendment scholars to adopt a conservative response, either by fundamentally questioning the value of false factual content protected under Alvarez, or by seeking to distinguish deepfakes from such constitutionally protected falsehoods through adaptive doctrinal strategies.

However, if we see this transformation in the long term, there will actually be a silver lining. As deepfakes become further widespread and visual literacy is sufficiently cultivated, people will be more mentally and intellectually prepared for visual uptake. They will critically analyze the presented information and compare competing sources. This process will undermine the automatic credibility of visual representations, making them far less competitive in the marketplace. This marks the entry into Deepfake 2.0, where a new market equilibrium will be built: the competitiveness of three information forms converges as people treat visual materials equivalent to factual statements, and even to subjective, unfalsifiable normative opinions. This benign “convergence” may trigger a more lenient approach to address deepfakes’ eligibility for First Amendment protection.

Our transtemporal examination of the inter-informational competitive dynamics enables us to conclude that the prevalence of deepfakes, as well as resulting “convergence,” is simply bringing us back to the Pre-Visual Age. The worst case under Deepfake 2.0 is the regression of truth certainty to the level of the Pre-Visual Age. Although such a regression is undesirable, it does not warrant excessive alarm. In preparing for Deepfake 2.0, it is worth reflecting on how our predecessors in the Pre-Visual Age navigated an age with uncertainties and continuously cultivated wisdom. In this sense, deepfaith in human resilience and intelligence remains the most powerful weapon against the challenges posed by deepfakes.

detail.title: Information and Communication Technologies and Employees Productivity in the Public Sector of Nigeria
detail.abstract: This study delves into the impact of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in enhancing employees' productivity in the public sector of Nigeria, focusing on technology adoption rates, training programs, e-learning platforms, digital communications, and social media engagement. Primary data was collected from the Ministry of Finance, Budget, and Economic Planning in Nigeria's six geopolitical zones using a closed-ended questionnaire administered on 450 employees. The analysis, employing descriptive, Pearson correlation, factor, and multiple regression methods, reveals notable findings. Technology adoption program exhibits a positive effect, significantly impacting work productivity and quality service, while showing non-significant effects on innovativeness. Similarly, technology training program significantly influences innovativeness, work productivity, and quality service. The usage of elearning platforms demonstrates a positive and significant impact on innovativeness, work productivity, and quality service. Digital communication also significantly contributes to enhanced employees' productivity across the mentioned constructs. In conclusion, the study establishes a statistically positive effect of technology in enhancing employees' productivity in the public sector of Nigeria. Based on these findings, recommendations include providing modern technology tools to employees post-training, fostering increased productivity. Additionally, promoting the use of e-learning platforms is suggested to facilitate continuous learning and skill development among employees.

title: The Non-Existent Equity Risk Premium in Brazil: Why the Stock Market is Not a True Real Asset
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Non-Existent Equity Risk Premium in Brazil: Why the Stock Market is Not a True Real Asset
detail.abstract: This essay argues that the Equity Risk Premium (ERP); the additional return expected from investing in equities over risk-free assets; does not reliably exist in Brazil. Over long historical periods, the Brazilian stock market has failed to deliver returns that adequately compensate for its elevated risk when compared to fixedincome alternatives. Consequently, the stock exchange in Brazil cannot be considered a "real asset" in the classical sense: one that intrinsically generates superior risk-adjusted value through participation in productive corporate growth. Drawing on institutional, historical, and comparative analysis, the discussion contrasts Brazil's experience with mature markets like the United States, highlighting structural impediments that erode any potential premium. The implications extend to investor behavior, financial theory, and public policy in emerging economies.

title: LLM Council with Double Delphi: An AI-Human Framework for Faculty Workload Policy Modelling
affiliations: State University of New York - Empire State University

detail.title: LLM Council with Double Delphi: An AI-Human Framework for Faculty Workload Policy Modelling
detail.abstract:
This working paper introduces and demonstrates an LLM Council with Double Delphi, a decision-support methodology that combines multi-model AI ensemble analysis with a classical Delphi-style human expert review to address complex policy questions. The approach is organized in two layers. In Phase One, multiple large language models independently analyze a shared problem, conduct targeted documentary research to identify relevant peer-comparison parameters, and propose candidate solutions. In Phase Two (beyond the scope of this paper), human domain experts review, challenge, and validate the AI synthesis, and may request additional data collection, revised assumptions, or a focused rerun of the AI analysis. 
We demonstrate Phase One through a faculty workload policy reform case at an adult-serving Open University (OU) within a State University System (SUS). Five frontier models (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, and Perplexity) worked independently and initially without access to one another's outputs. Despite this independence, the models converged on the same core results: a common workload anchor expressed as 704 Student Credit Hours annually (used as a transparent benchmarking baseline), a shared two-track reform structure, and a single critical assumption requiring empirical validation (the conversion factor used to value mentoring work). Methodologically, this study differs from prior "council" syntheses that rely on a single chair/captain: the researcher appointed three co-captains-Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude-to produce independent syntheses of the Phase One reports and jointly shape the final manuscript, enabling triangulation across summaries and clearer identification of consensus, disagreement, and validation needs.

title: Do Non-Compete Agreements Help or Hurt Workers? Evidence from the Nlsy97
affiliations: , Columbia University and Queen’s University

detail.title: Do Non-Compete Agreements Help or Hurt Workers? Evidence from the Nlsy97
detail.abstract: While non-compete agreements (NCs) are prevalent, the incentives driving their use and their causal effects on workers remain poorly understood. We develop a model with asymmetric information to show that NCs shift the nature of allocative inefficiency by reducing inefficient quits and increasing inefficient retention, while mitigating the canonical holdup problem. The model predicts that NCs are more likely to be used in industries with high returns on industry-specific investments, and that signers have longer job tenures, higher contracted wages, and receive more firm-provided investment than similar workers without such agreements. To test these predictions, we use panel data from the NLSY97 and a differencein-differences research design to estimate the causal impact of signing an NC. We find that NCs raise job tenures by 6% and lead to an immediate wage increase of 10%. Six years after signing, the wage premium falls to 5%. There is substantial heterogeneity, with non-White, non-college and lower-wage workers experiencing lower wage-growth after signing an NC. Consistent with the theory, NC usage is more prevalent among higher skilled workers who perform more sophisticated tasks and have higher returns on experience. While the theory links NCs to firm investment, we find no evidence of increased investment in formal training, suggesting investments prompted by the agreement are likely informal. Our findings caution against blanket bans on NC usage.

detail.abstract:
This article challenges the assumption that AI inevitably leads to the de-skilling of law students.  Some faculty understandably fear that students will use AI to bypass critical thinking and avoid meaningful effort.  This article reframes AI as a potential catalyst for improving legal education rather than inherently a threat.

Concerns about de-skilling generally are based on the assumption that faculty will not change traditional writing assignments.  This article analyzes why these assignments often fail to help students develop strong analytical and writing skills. These include limited instruction in basic writing skills, poor design, lack of feedback, and faculty inertia in the face of rapid technological change.  

This article recommends replacing long, end-of-semester papers with a sequence of short assignments culminating in concise papers modeled on bar association journal articles.  This approach should improve student analytical and writing skills, reduce incentives to misuse AI, and prepare students for the writing tasks they are likely to do in practice.  Faculty can use this assignment with or without allowing students to use AI.  If faculty teach students to use AI responsibly, both students and faculty can become more "AI literate."

title: The Raid on Somnath: Ghaznavid Ambitions and Divine Destiny in Futuh-us-Salatain

detail.title: The Raid on Somnath: Ghaznavid Ambitions and Divine Destiny in Futuh-us-Salatain
detail.abstract:
Futuh-us-Salatain, meaning Gifts of the Sultans, is a 14th-century work written by Abdul Malik Isami, approximately 2-3 centuries after the raids of Mahmud of Ghazni. Isami referred to it as the Shahnama-i-Hind (The Shahnameh of India). In his account, Isami cites various legends and reports from his contemporaries and acquaintances as his sources. While the work provides valuable insights into the historical narrative of the period, its historical reliability is often questioned due to factual inaccuracies. Moreover, Isami's interpretation of events suggests that he viewed them as preordained by divine will or destiny, influencing his understanding of the unfolding history.

In Futuh-us-Salatin, the author offers a detailed and vivid account of Mahmud of Ghazni’s incursions into India, portraying him in a glorified light. Mahmud is depicted as a warrior of unparalleled zeal, one who made the blood of the infidels flow like the Euphrates and achieved feats no ruler before him had dared. The destruction of the grand idol house of Somnath is extolled as a singular triumph, an act of piety and power that no predecessor had accomplished.

title: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for Portfolio Selection: A Comparative Study with Classical Markowitz Optimization
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for Portfolio Selection: A Comparative Study with Classical Markowitz Optimization
detail.abstract: Portfolio optimization is a fundamental problem in quantitative finance and is traditionally addressed using the classical Markowitz mean-variance model. Although this approach has proven effective, the inclusion of discrete constraints such as cardinality limits or binary asset selection introduces significant computational complexity, motivating the exploration of QUBO-based formulations and variational quantum algorithms. In this work, we formulate a small-scale portfolio selection instance as a QUBO model, which is mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian and solved using the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). We implement QAOA on a quantum simulator and compare its performance with a classical solver for the same QUBO problem. Markowitz is used only as a conceptual framework that motivates the problem formulation, but not as a numerical baseline, since the classical continuous model is not directly comparable with the discrete version used here. The main contribution of this study is a detailed educational explanation of QAOA, its components, the circuit structure, and the variational scheme, together with an applied demonstration in a financial context. Rather than claiming quantum advantage, the focus is on understanding the algorithm's behavior in realistic small-scale instances. Finally, we discuss whether, as quantum technology advances, QAOA could provide practical benefits in portfolio optimization or whether classical methods will remain sufficient in practice.

title: Deploying Artificial Intelligence in India: A 12-Month Policy Roadmap Informed by Global Best Practices
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Deploying Artificial Intelligence in India: A 12-Month Policy Roadmap Informed by Global Best Practices
detail.abstract: India stands at a pivotal juncture in its artificial intelligence (AI) journey, with the potential to harness AI for transformative socioeconomic impact. As global AI policy frameworks rapidly evolve, India has launched its own AI Governance Guidelines, emphasizing innovation, inclusion, and responsible deployment. However, to fully realize AI's promise, India must enact a comprehensive, phased policy package over the next twelve months-one that integrates global best practices in regulation, ethics, data governance, and public-private partnerships, while addressing India's unique challenges and opportunities. This whitepaper synthesizes the current state of global AI policy, analyzes recent international developments, and proposes a detailed, actionable roadmap for India's AI deployment, ensuring ethical, scalable, and inclusive growth.

title: Contracts-for-Difference and Nuclear Flexibility: A Path to Complementing Renewables
affiliations: CentraleSupélec and Carnegie Mellon University

detail.title: Contracts-for-Difference and Nuclear Flexibility: A Path to Complementing Renewables
detail.abstract: Contracts-for-Difference (CfDs) shift the electricity price risk from producers to third parties, typically governments, and have been instrumental in fostering renewable energy investment in liberalized electricity markets. As Western countries turn to CfDs to support new nuclear power plant (NPP) investments, concerns arise regarding their impact on short-term dispatch. By shielding producers from real-time wholesale prices, CfDs can distort dispatch incentives, leading to inefficiencies. Innovative CfD designs have been proposed in the literature to mitigate these effects, some of which have already materialized in some countries. This paper assesses how different CfD designs influence nuclear dispatch decisions in a projected 2040 Central Western Europe electricity market. Using a partial equilibrium model formulated as a Mathematical Program with Equilibrium Constraints (MPEC) and solved as a Mixed Integer Quadratically Constrained Program (MIQCP), we reveal unintended consequences. Notably, a CfD with negative-price interruption can induce NPP operators to reduce availability in moments of soaring prices, resulting in higher general prices than the first-best solution. This results from nuclear plants' limited flexibility: operators must balance producing at low output levels during negative prices with maximizing production at other times to secure the strike price. We show how a non-production-based CfD design can partially alleviate this problem and improve NPPs' short-term dispatch, although we show the latter cannot restore the optimal dispatch either. These findings emphasize the critical importance of careful CfD design and ongoing regulatory oversight as governments expand CfD applications to nuclear power.

title: Leveraging the Power of AI: Efficiency in Business

detail.abstract: The dissertation aimed to examine how leading companies are adopting artificial intelligence capabilities like machine learning, natural language processing, and predictive analytics to optimize operations, lower costs, and enhance data-driven decision making. An extensive analysis of academic articles, industry reports, and real-world case studies provided insights on the AI techniques, implementation strategies, and organizational capabilities enabling firms to achieve productivity improvements. Findings revealed common AI applications boosting business efficiency across core functions like intelligent process automation in manufacturing and customer service, predictive planning and forecasting in supply chain and marketing, personalized recommendation systems for customers, and conversational AI assistants that can handle employee queries. However, the research highlighted that maximizing AI's benefits requires holistic integration with complementary organizational changes in skills, culture, workflows, and responsible governance. The dissertation put forth a conceptual framework analysing the impact of factors like depth of AI adoption, training data quality, and human-AI collaboration on efficiency gains. Through qualitative and quantitative analysis, it assessed tactical metrics like cost reductions along with strategic performance indicators to evaluate AI success. AI implementation best practices emerged around use case piloting, managing change, and workforce augmentation. Overall, the dissertation synthesized scattered knowledge on pragmatic AI adoption for elevating business productivity into an applied framework grounded in evidence. It provides technology leaders and managers an actionable playbook to thoughtfully harness AI's potential within their organizational contexts, while upholding ethical principles, for sustainable competitive advantage.

title: Telework adoption and CO2 emissions: analysis from the Lisbon Metropolitan Area

detail.title: Telework adoption and CO2 emissions: analysis from the Lisbon Metropolitan Area
detail.abstract: Climate change is a major global challenge, intensified by rising greenhouse gas emissions and private car dependence. Travel demand management (TDM) strategies aim to mitigate negative transport externalities of excessive motorisation. Telework, emerged in the 1970s with Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs), has been discussed as a potential TDM tool to reduce commute, congestion, and emissions. Although its effects on travel behaviour remain controversial, interest grew with COVID-19 pandemic, and a hybrid telework regime is likely to consolidate as a common arrangement. This study examines the impact of telework engagement (both full- and part-day) on total weekly CO2 emissions in the Lisbon Metropolitan Area. Structural Equation Modelling results indicate that full-day telework reduces CO2 emissions, while part-day telework may slightly increase them. Overall, telework can support climate change mitigation, but its benefits may be offset by urban sprawl and longer commute distances, depending on telework regime and frequency.

title: CFD-Driven Optimization and Numerical Validation of Cargo Hold Fan Automatic Control

detail.title: CFD-Driven Optimization and Numerical Validation of Cargo Hold Fan Automatic Control
detail.abstract: Aiming at the industry pain point of excessive energy consumption caused by the traditional constant-power operation of cargo hold fans in refrigerated container ships, combined with the development needs of green ships and intelligent control, this study proposes a dual-speed automatic control scheme for cargo hold fans based on Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) technology.[1] Taking the 4th to 6th cargo holds of a container ship as the research object, temperature sensors are arranged in zones to collect in-hold environmental parameters, and the intelligent switching of fan speed (high/low) is realized relying on the Integrated Control and Monitoring System (ICMS). A three-dimensional flow field model of the cargo hold is constructed using CFD technology to simulate the temperature field and velocity distribution under three typical refrigerated container loading conditions (lower layer, middle layer, and upper layer loading), verifying the feasibility and energy-saving effect of the control scheme. The results show that on the premise of meeting the cargo hold temperature control requirement of 45°C, the total energy consumption of the fans in low-speed operation is only 30% of that in high-speed operation, which significantly reduces the ship operation cost. [2]This research provides theoretical support and engineering reference for the energy-saving optimization and intelligent upgrading of the ventilation system in refrigerated container ships.

detail.abstract: Biodiversity loss is increasingly identified as a potential threat to human rights. In the absence of any references to biodiversity in human rights treaties and the near absence from constitutions, biodiversity can be protected by the nearly universally recognised right to a healthy environment. But can this right be used to protect biodiversity in the context of another global environmental problem, climate change? To answer this question, this Chapter analyses three cases in Colombia, Nepal, and Norway, where the claimants invoked a constitutionally recognised right to a healthy environment when they challenged the respective governments on climate change grounds, and where the courts considered the impacts on biodiversity. title: Breaking the Boundary of Queuing: The Value and Spatial Externality of Virtual Queuing
affiliations: , Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of  Management, University of Surrey and Hong Kong Polytechnic University - Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies

detail.title: Breaking the Boundary of Queuing: The Value and Spatial Externality of Virtual Queuing
detail.abstract: Virtual queuing allows customers to join virtually rather than physically and monitor their queue status remotely, reshaping waiting experiences and further improving customer satisfaction. We investigate the impact of virtual queuing adoption on customer satisfaction of focal restaurants (i.e., adopters) and explore its spatial externalities on neighboring restaurants. Leveraging a large-scale panel dataset from Dianping.com (2019–2024), we employ a difference-in-differences (DID) approach combined with propensity score matching (PSM) to identify the causal effects of virtual queuing adoption. Results show that virtual queuing improves customer satisfaction at focal restaurants and generate positive spillover effects for nearby merchants. Further analysis reveals important spatial mechanisms. First, we find that more substantial direct benefits from virtual queuing impact restaurants located outside service clusters, while those located in clusters benefit more from spillover effects. Moreover, diverse, less concentrated and dense clusters tend to dilute the main effect for adopters but amplify the overall positive impact across the cluster. These findings indicate the dual role of virtual queuing—as a firm-level innovation that enhances operational performance and as a spatially embedded digital tool that shapes competitive intensity - highlights the critical role of spatial proximity in shaping co-opetition in the service industry.

title: The Effect of Economic Value Added (EVA) and Profitability Ratios on Stock Returns: Evidence from Food and Beverage Companies Listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange

detail.abstract: This study examines the effect of Economic Value Added (EVA) and profitability ratios on stock returns of food and beverage companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) from 2005 to 2009. The research aims to determine whether EVA, Return on Assets (ROA), and Return on Equity (ROE) can explain variations in stock return performance, both individually and simultaneously. The sample consists of 17 companies that consistently published audited financial statements during the observation period. Multiple regression analysis was used to test the relationship between the variables. The findings reveal that EVA, ROA, and ROE jointly have a significant effect on stock returns, while individually, only ROA shows a positive and significant influence. The results suggest that traditional accounting measures, particularly ROA, remain more reliable indicators of stock return performance than EVA. This study contributes to the understanding of performance measurement and value creation in Indonesia's capital market, especially for investors and policymakers in emerging economies.

title: Good Intentions, Harmful Consequences: When and How Leader Health Symbolization Becomes Moral Hypocrisy
affiliations: , , Macau University of Science and Technology, ,  and Sun Yat-sen University

detail.title: Good Intentions, Harmful Consequences: When and How Leader Health Symbolization Becomes Moral Hypocrisy
detail.abstract: Employee health is critical for both individual happiness and organizational sustainability. Despite organizations implementing comprehensive health-care policies, employees still report significant health challenges. To address this persistent gap, leaders often demonstrate valuing health in the workplace as a form of symbolization, aiming to benefit employee health. However, we challenge the prevailing positive expectations of leader health symbolization by drawing on behavioral integrity theory. We propose that such symbolic actions may have unintended negative consequences under certain conditions. The findings from an experimental study and a field study reveal that employees experiencing high workloads may perceive leader health symbolization as moral hypocrisy and, in turn, are more likely to engage in workplace deviance. In sum, by uncovering the unintended consequences of leader health symbolization, this research provides a more nuanced and balanced understanding of the leader’s role in organizational health management.

detail.abstract: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) is now a fundamental part of modern business strategy, crucial for boosting reputation and productivity. This study investigates the relationship between CSR and working performance (WP) within the service industry, employing the PLS-SEM structural model for analysis. The findings confirm that CSR significantly and positively impacts WP. Moreover, this positive effect is amplified by two key mediating factors: Transformational Leadership Style (LTR) and Employee Satisfaction (SAT). The research recommends that enterprises should prioritize CSR initiatives and adopt a transformational leadership approach that actively supports employee welfare and development. By doing so, businesses can maximize the beneficial influence of CSR on WP, thereby enhancing their competitiveness and improving employee well-being through the implementation of effective and sustainable CSR strategies.
